# Education in Sweden
Sweden’s education system is structured into several levels: preschool (förskola, ages 1–6), a one-year preschool class (förskoleklass, ages 6–7), nine years of compulsory school (grundskola, ages 7–16), optional three-year upper secondary school (gymnasieskola, ages 16–19), and higher education provided by universities and university colleges. Compulsory education includes a broad curriculum of 16 subjects, with grades awarded from year 6 onwards, and national tests given in grades 3, 6, and 9. At the upper secondary level, nearly all students continue their studies in one of 18 national programmes, split into preparatory and vocational tracks, with entry dependent on core subject proficiency. Students must complete a diploma project, and qualification for higher education requires completion of preparatory programmes or specific vocational tracks.
Higher education follows the Bologna Process, offering Bachelor's, Master's, and Doctoral degrees with varying entry requirements. Swedish instruction and English proficiency are mandatory for university admission. The grading systems vary among institutions but are criteria-referenced and compatible with European standards. Publicly funded independent (free) schools have proliferated since the 1990s, comprising a significant portion of enrolment and offering alternate pedagogies or special profiles; their profit model and impact on educational standards are subjects of ongoing debate. Sweden participates in international assessments such as PISA and PIRLS, with fluctuating performance noted over the past decades. The state provides student aid via loans and grants, and higher education remains free for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens. Education policy emphasizes anti-discrimination and universal access, and adult education or introductory programmes accommodate those not meeting traditional requirements.
